html:
This shape marks Nahua speakers in western Mexico, around the coast and hills of Colima and southern Jalisco. The Nahuas are the largest Indigenous people of Mexico, and their language, Nahuatl, was also that of the Aztecs.

The west was never ruled by the Aztecs. In the 1400s it was a land of small chiefdoms, squeezed between the powerful Purépecha kingdom of Michoacán to the east and the peoples of the Nayarit mountains, such as the Huichol, to the north. People here farmed maize, made salt on the coast and grew cacao and cotton.

Spanish soldiers took Colima in 1523, and the area became part of New Spain. Disease cut the population sharply in the next decades. Small Nahua communities still live in the region. See also Nahua (Mexico).
